explanation: Fires on modal/auxiliary verbs, chiefly 'may' (also 'might', 'must', 'will'), right after a subject noun or pronoun, e.g. 'you may not use this file' in Apache license headers, 'That may sound', 'a bullet may come'. Some strong hits are on Hungarian case suffixes ('-ból', '-ra') and the Spanish auxiliary 'han'. Other tokens give weak, scattered activation.

Fires on function words and word-start subword pieces inside German and Scandinavian (Danish/Norwegian) text: prepositions and particles like 'zu', 'auf', 'für', 'von', 'til', 'på', 'et', 'er', and prefix fragments like 'gesch', 'Auf', 'ange', 'Sønder'. It fires most strongly in running German/Danish sentences, weakly on Germanic-looking names or abbreviations inside English, and is near zero on ordinary English text.

Mixed. Its strongest jobs are the 'super' keyword in object-oriented code ('[super init...]', 'super.viewDidLoad()', 'super.clone()') and the final subword piece of country or demonym names ('Samo|an', 'Turkmen|istan', 'Sierra Leone', 'F|ij|ian'). It also fires on scientific word fragments ('decom|pression', 'ser|pin', 'ty|ros|ine') and on citation-reference fragments ('@R2', '@REF2').

Fires mainly on the return type 'void' in Java/C# method declarations, strongest in 'public static void main' and somewhat weaker for 'public void setX(...)'. There is also scattered activation on unrelated tokens (e.g. 'syst|olic', 'COPYRIGHT', '@data|class', 'OutOf|Memory').

No clear unifying feature. It fires on the token before a number in counts or statistics (a space before a numeral, '=' in '16*1.5= 24', a decimal point), on the start of surnames ('Sch'), and on assorted content words in expository prose ('other', 'that', 'can', 'result'). It looks like a diffuse mixture.

Its strongest hits are digits inside long runs of zeros ('0000000'). Moderate hits include the last token of standard boilerplate ('limitations under the License'), namespace/domain suffixes ('System.Text', 'jsfiddle.net', 'errors.New'), the exponent in 'f^{-1}', 'oste|opor|osis', and surnames after given names. It seems to respond to highly predictable completions of a fixed sequence, but the examples are heterogeneous.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces (stems or suffixes) of morphologically rich non-English words, especially Hungarian, Russian, Finnish, Turkish and German (e.g. 'szolgáltat|ás|ra', 'ути|лит|ой', 'совет|ами', 'Daten|bank'). It is weaker on other languages and near zero on English.

Broad and diffuse. It fires on structural tokens in code and config text, such as connection-string keys ('Port', 'port'), path separators and segments ('/versioned', '\', '/meta'), the ':' before a port number, digits in patent numbers, and indentation tabs. It also fires on scattered words in prose ('danger', 'women', 'car'). There is no single clear concept.

No coherent pattern. Strong hits include C preprocessor tokens ('#include', '#define'), camelCase identifier pieces ('extract|Data', 'log|Level', 'With|Exception'), LaTeX '\frac', court-opinion line breaks, and assorted English words ('her', 'never', 'cannot', 'female', 'if'). It looks polysemantic.

Fires on whitespace, newlines and formatting tokens at document-structure boundaries, especially in legal/court documents (indentation or newlines after 'Circuit Judges.', after case citations like '37 F.3d 477', 'Before', 'TABLE OF CONTENTS'), as well as code indentation, wire-dateline '--', '{#sec:intro}' markers, table borders and '-----Original Message-----'. It responds to layout/section-break positions rather than to content words.

Fires on the first or a middle subword piece of rare, multi-token proper nouns, mostly foreign place names, company or drug names and personal names (e.g. 'Gl|ax|oSmithKline', 'U|dz|ungwa', 'Psych|od|idae', 'Can|averal', 'Tam|iflu', 'Ind|raprastha'). The model is mid-way through spelling out an unfamiliar name. It is weak on common words.

Fires on tokens about 3D or spatial dimensions. The strongest is the ' x' separator in dimension specs ('110mm x 110mm x 8mm'). It also fires on '3D'/'3d', the third coordinate or comma in xyz triples, 'non-planar', 'depth', 'cylinder', 'rotateZ', 'vertical' and 'R^3'.

Fires on the token right after the city/location in a news dateline, usually the ' (' before the wire-service or station name ('WASHINGTON (AP)', 'LONDON (Reuters)', 'PEORIA, Ill. (WEEK)'), less strongly on a comma there ('TORONTO, June 5'). It is moderately active on similar boilerplate document openings such as 'The present invention relates to' in patents and court-case header punctuation.

Fires on words about mixing or mixtures ('mixed', 'mix', 'mixture', 'Mixi', 'stirring', 'liquid-solid') and on the token just before such a word or a compound ('stream of [mixed fuel and air]', 'with a [mixture]', 'consisting of a [...]'). It is strongest for physical or chemical mixtures and moderate for figurative ones ('mixed evidence', 'mixed cultures').
